solution:
For a nonvolatile solute Raoult's law gives the vapour pressure of the solution as \(P_1 = P_1^0 x_1\), where \(x_1\) is the mole fraction of the SOLVENT.

Moles of water \(n_1 = 2\), moles of solute \(n_2 = 2\), so

\(x_1 = \dfrac{2}{2 + 2} = 0.5\)

\(P_1 = 24\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} \times 0.5 = 12\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

Why the other options fail: 24 mm Hg is the vapour pressure of PURE water, which the solution can never reach once a nonvolatile solute is dissolved; 48 mm Hg is \(24/x_1\), i.e. dividing by the mole fraction instead of multiplying, and a solution's vapour pressure can never exceed that of the pure solvent; 32 mm Hg corresponds to no mole fraction obtainable from 2 mol of solute in 2 mol of water.

A colligative property is a property of a solution that depends only on the NUMBER of solute particles and not on their nature. The chapter lists exactly four: vapour pressure LOWERING, boiling point ELEVATION, freezing point DEPRESSION and OSMOTIC PRESSURE.

Osmotic pressure is the only one of the four listed options that is itself a colligative property, because it is defined for the solution and is proportional to the concentration of solute particles: \(\pi = MRT\).

Why the other options fail: vapour pressure, boiling point and freezing point are properties a pure solvent already possesses; each depends on the identity of the liquid, not on any solute count. What is colligative in those three cases is the CHANGE produced by the solute — the lowering, the elevation and the depression — not the quantity itself.

The working equation for osmotic pressure is \(\pi = MRT\), where \(M\) is MOLARITY (moles of solute per \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) of solution). The chapter states the reason explicitly: osmotic pressure measurements are made at one fixed temperature, so there is no need for a temperature-independent concentration unit.

Why the other options fail: molality is preferred for boiling point elevation and freezing point depression, where the temperature CHANGES during the measurement, so it is the wrong unit here; mole fraction and mass percent do not appear in \(\pi = MRT\) at all and cannot be substituted into it.

Boiling point elevation obeys \(\Delta T_b = K_b m\), where \(m\) is the molality of the solution. Putting \(m = 1\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\) gives \(\Delta T_b = K_b\).

So the ebullioscopic (molal elevation) constant is numerically the boiling point elevation of a ONE MOLAL solution — option a, \(1m\).

Why the other options fail: \(1M\) is one molar, a per-litre-of-solution unit that does not appear in \(\Delta T_b = K_b m\); 1 mass% and unit mole fraction of solute are concentration measures the equation is not written in, and substituting either into it would not return \(K_b\).

The cryoscopic constant \(K_f\) is the freezing point depression produced by a one molal solution, \(\Delta T_f = K_f m\). Its value is fixed by the solvent alone — water has \(K_f = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\) whatever is dissolved in it.

Why the other options fail: the nature of the solute cannot enter, because freezing point depression is a colligative property that counts particles and ignores their identity; "nature of solution" would make \(K_f\) change from one solute to another, which contradicts the same principle; and the number of solvent molecules is a measure of how much solvent is present, whereas \(K_f\) is an intensive constant that does not change with the amount taken.

Dissolving a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapour pressure, so the solution must be heated to a HIGHER temperature than the pure solvent before its vapour pressure reaches 1 atm. Hence \(T_b > T_b^0\): the boiling point of the solvent is lower than that of the solution, which is option b.

Why the other options fail: (a) is the exact reverse of vapour pressure lowering — \(P_1 < P_1^0\), so the solution's vapour pressure is LOWER than the pure solvent's; (c) is wrong because osmotic pressure is defined only for a solution separated from its solvent, and the solvent side contributes none, so a solution's osmotic pressure cannot be the lower of the two; (d) confuses the process with the property — the chapter's list of colligative properties names OSMOTIC PRESSURE, whereas osmosis is the flow of solvent through the membrane, not a measurable property of the solution.

The cell contents are isotonic with 0.3 M sugar, and sugar does not dissociate, so the osmotic pressure INSIDE the cell is

\(\pi_{\text{in}} = MRT = 0.3 \times 0.0821 \times 310 = 7.64\ \mathrm{atm}\)

KCl dissociates completely into \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\), so \(i = 2\) and the OUTSIDE solution exerts

\(\pi_{\text{out}} = iMRT = 2 \times 0.1 \times 0.0821 \times 310 = 5.09\ \mathrm{atm}\)

The outside solution is therefore hypotonic to the cell, solvent enters the cell, and the osmotic pressure that develops across the membrane is the difference

\(\pi = 7.64 - 5.09 = 2.54\ \mathrm{atm}\)

Why the other options fail: 5.08 atm is \(\pi_{\text{out}}\) alone, which is a property the KCl solution already had before the cell was placed in it and would leave the whole first sentence of the question unused; 4.92 atm and 2.46 atm are the same two quantities evaluated at 300 K instead of body temperature, 310 K.

[Note: the four printed options are degenerate — because \(0.3 - 0.2 = 0.1\) and \(0.3 - 0.1 = 0.2\), the same four numbers arise whether one computes the osmotic pressure of the KCl solution or the difference across the membrane, so the option set alone cannot settle the reading. This answer takes "what osmotic pressure DEVELOPS when the cell is placed in the solution" as the pressure arising across the membrane, which is the only reading that uses the given 0.3 M sugar data. A student who answered 5.08 atm has computed \(\pi_{\text{out}}\) correctly, including the van't Hoff factor.]

Isotonic means the glucose solution has the same osmotic pressure as blood, 7.65 atm at 310 K. Glucose is a nonelectrolyte, so \(i = 1\) and \(\pi = MRT\):

\(M = \dfrac{\pi}{RT} = \dfrac{7.65}{0.0821 \times 310} = 0.3006\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\)

Molar mass of glucose \(\mathrm{(C_6H_{12}O_6)}\) is 180 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\), so one litre of solution contains

\(0.3006 \times 180 = 54.1\ \mathrm{g}\)

That is 5.41 g per 100 mL, i.e. 5.41 %.

Why the other options fail: 53.4 % is the same figure with the decimal point moved one place, i.e. grams per litre reported as a percentage; 3.54 % and 4.53 % are digit rearrangements of the correct value and follow from no consistent substitution into \(\pi = MRT\) with \(M_{\text{glucose}} = 180\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\).

Raoult's law for a solution of a nonvolatile solute is \(P_1 = P_1^0 x_1\), where \(x_1\) is the mole fraction of the SOLVENT and \(P_1^0\) is a constant at a given temperature. The vapour pressure of the solution is therefore DIRECTLY proportional to the mole fraction of the solvent — option d.

Why the other options fail: (a) reverses the roles — writing \(P_1 \propto x_2\) would make the vapour pressure rise as more solute is added, whereas it falls; (b) and (c) are inverse proportionalities, which would send the vapour pressure to infinity as \(x_2 \to 0\) (b) or as \(x_1 \to 0\) (c), and the correct relation is the linear one, with \(P_1 = P_1^0\) at \(x_1 = 1\) and \(P_1 = 0\) at \(x_1 = 0\).

A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the applied pressure. Inside a pressure cooker the applied pressure is well above 1 atm, so water must be heated past \(100^\circ\mathrm{C}\) before it boils. Cooking then proceeds at a higher temperature, and the rate of the chemical and physical changes involved in cooking rises with temperature, so the food cooks faster.

Why the other options fail: (b) heat distribution is no more even in a cooker than in a covered pan, and evenness would not shorten the total cooking time; (c) the pressure inside a domestic cooker is only about 2 atm, far too small to crush food, and mechanical crushing is not what cooks it; (d) cooking does involve chemical changes, but this option names the changes rather than the reason the COOKER is faster — the raised boiling point is what supplies the higher temperature.

[Textbook misprint: the stem prints the units of the Henry's law constant as \(\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\ atm}\). As printed \(\mathrm{K_H}P\) would carry units \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ atm^{2}}\), which is not a concentration; the constant is \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ atm^{-1}}\), as used above and as the chapter defines it in section 2.4.1.]

Henry's law states \(S = \mathrm{K_H}P\), where \(S\) is the solubility of the gas and \(P\) its partial pressure over the solution.

\(S = 0.159\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ atm^{-1}} \times 0.164\ \mathrm{atm} = 0.0261\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}} \approx 0.026\ \mathrm{M}\)

Why the other options fail: 0.0159 \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\) is the Henry's law constant itself with the decimal point moved, not a solubility; 0.164 \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\) is the partial pressure quoted as if it were a concentration; 0.042 \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\) is close to \(P/\mathrm{K_H} \times 0.04\) and follows from no correct use of \(S = \mathrm{K_H}P\) — note that dividing rather than multiplying gives 1.03 M, which is not offered.

Both urea and sucrose are nonelectrolytes, so \(i = 1\) for each and \(\pi = MRT\) depends on molarity alone. At the same temperature the 0.1 M urea solution has twice the osmotic pressure of the 0.05 M sucrose solution.

Isotonic solutions are defined as solutions having the SAME osmotic pressure. These two do not, so statement c is the one that is NOT correct, and it is the required answer.

Why the other options are correct statements, and so cannot be the answer: (a) is true, since \(0.1 > 0.05\) and \(\pi \propto M\); (b) is true, since the more concentrated solution with the higher osmotic pressure is by definition the hypertonic one; (d) is true and is simply (b) stated from the other side — the more dilute sucrose solution is hypotonic to the urea solution.
